lessons.title: Qiskit Runtime & Primitives
lessons.content:
Qiskit Runtime & Primitives

💡 The New Execution Model

Qiskit Runtime brings computation closer to the quantum hardware, reducing latency. Primitives (Sampler & Estimator) provide a high-level interface for common quantum tasks.

Why Qiskit Runtime?

Traditional Execution

  • Send circuit to cloud
  • Wait in queue
  • Execute
  • Return results
  • Repeat for each iteration

High latency for iterative algorithms

Qiskit Runtime

  • Send program once
  • Classical logic runs near QPU
  • Multiple iterations without queuing
  • Return final results

10-100x faster for VQE/QAOA

The Primitives

Sampler

Samples probability distributions from quantum circuits

Output: Quasi-probability distributions

Estimator

Computes expectation values of observables

Output: ⟨ψ|O|ψ⟩ values

Using Sampler

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.primitives import Sampler

# Create a Bell state circuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.measure_all()

# Use Sampler
sampler = Sampler()
job = sampler.run(qc, shots=1000)
result = job.result()

# Get quasi-probabilities
quasi_dists = result.quasi_dists[0]
print(f"Quasi-distribution: {quasi_dists}")
# Expected: {0: 0.5, 3: 0.5} for |00⟩ and |11⟩

Using Estimator

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.primitives import Estimator
from qiskit.quantum_info import SparsePauliOp

# Create circuit (no measurement!)
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)

# Define observable
observable = SparsePauliOp.from_list([
    ("ZZ", 1.0),
    ("XX", 0.5)
])

# Use Estimator
estimator = Estimator()
job = estimator.run(qc, observable)
result = job.result()

expectation_value = result.values[0]
print(f"⟨ZZ + 0.5*XX⟩ = {expectation_value}")

Batch Execution

# Run multiple circuits at once
circuits = [qc1, qc2, qc3]
observables = [obs1, obs2, obs3]

estimator = Estimator()
job = estimator.run(circuits, observables)
results = job.result()

# All expectation values
for i, val in enumerate(results.values):
    print(f"Circuit {i}: ⟨O⟩ = {val}")

💡 Best Practices

  • Use Estimator for VQE/QAOA (expectation values)
  • Use Sampler for sampling algorithms (Grover, QAOA final)
  • Batch circuits when possible for efficiency
  • Use Runtime sessions for iterative algorithms
keyTakeaways: Qiskit Runtime executes classical logic near the QPU
Sampler returns probability distributions from circuits
Estimator computes observable expectation values
Primitives enable efficient batch execution

lessons.title: Error Mitigation Techniques
lessons.content:
Error Mitigation Techniques

💡 NISQ Era Solution

Error mitigation reduces the impact of noise without requiring error correction. These techniques use classical post-processing to improve result accuracy on noisy devices.

Error Correction vs Mitigation

Error Correction

  • Requires many physical qubits
  • Syndrome measurements
  • Real-time feedback
  • Eliminates errors

Error Mitigation

  • Works with existing qubits
  • Classical post-processing
  • Multiple circuit executions
  • Reduces error effects

Key Mitigation Techniques

Measurement Error Mitigation

Corrects readout errors using calibration matrix

Run calibration circuits, invert error matrix

Zero Noise Extrapolation (ZNE)

Amplify noise, then extrapolate to zero noise

Run at multiple noise levels, fit curve

Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC)

Sample from quasi-probability representation

High overhead but unbiased

Twirled Readout Error eXtinction (TREX)

Randomized benchmarking for readout

Built into Qiskit Runtime

Measurement Error Mitigation

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
from qiskit_aer.noise import NoiseModel, ReadoutError
import numpy as np

# Create noisy simulator
noise_model = NoiseModel()
readout_error = ReadoutError([[0.95, 0.05], [0.1, 0.9]])  # P(0|0)=0.95, P(1|1)=0.9
noise_model.add_all_qubit_readout_error(readout_error)

# Calibration circuits
def get_calibration_matrix(n_qubits, backend, shots=1000):
    """Measure the readout error matrix"""
    cal_matrix = np.zeros((2**n_qubits, 2**n_qubits))
    
    for i in range(2**n_qubits):
        # Prepare computational basis state |i⟩
        qc = QuantumCircuit(n_qubits)
        for j in range(n_qubits):
            if (i >> j) & 1:
                qc.x(j)
        qc.measure_all()
        
        result = backend.run(qc, shots=shots).result()
        counts = result.get_counts()
        
        for measured, count in counts.items():
            m = int(measured, 2)
            cal_matrix[m, i] = count / shots
    
    return cal_matrix

def mitigate_counts(counts, cal_matrix):
    """Apply readout error mitigation"""
    n_states = cal_matrix.shape[0]
    raw_probs = np.zeros(n_states)
    
    total = sum(counts.values())
    for state, count in counts.items():
        raw_probs[int(state, 2)] = count / total
    
    # Invert calibration matrix
    inv_cal = np.linalg.pinv(cal_matrix)
    mitigated_probs = inv_cal @ raw_probs
    
    # Clip negative probabilities
    mitigated_probs = np.clip(mitigated_probs, 0, 1)
    mitigated_probs /= mitigated_probs.sum()
    
    return {format(i, f'0{int(np.log2(n_states))}b'): p 
            for i, p in enumerate(mitigated_probs) if p > 0.001}

# Example usage
backend = AerSimulator(noise_model=noise_model)
cal_matrix = get_calibration_matrix(2, backend)
print("Calibration matrix:")
print(cal_matrix)

Zero Noise Extrapolation

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import curve_fit

def amplify_noise(circuit, scale_factor):
    """Amplify noise by repeating gates"""
    amplified = circuit.copy()
    for _ in range(scale_factor - 1):
        # Add gate and its inverse to amplify noise
        for gate in circuit.data:
            amplified.append(gate[0], gate[1])
            amplified.append(gate[0].inverse(), gate[1])
            amplified.append(gate[0], gate[1])
    return amplified

def zero_noise_extrapolation(circuit, observable, backend, scale_factors=[1, 2, 3]):
    """Extrapolate to zero noise"""
    results = []
    
    for scale in scale_factors:
        amp_circuit = amplify_noise(circuit, scale)
        # Run and get expectation value
        # (simplified - would use Estimator in practice)
        exp_val = run_and_measure(amp_circuit, observable, backend)
        results.append(exp_val)
    
    # Fit exponential decay and extrapolate
    def exp_decay(x, a, b, c):
        return a * np.exp(-b * x) + c
    
    popt, _ = curve_fit(exp_decay, scale_factors, results)
    zero_noise_value = exp_decay(0, *popt)
    
    return zero_noise_value

💡 Qiskit Runtime Integration

Qiskit Runtime Estimator has built-in error mitigation options:

options = {"resilience_level": 2}  # Enable ZNE
estimator = Estimator(options=options)
keyTakeaways: Error mitigation reduces noise effects without correction qubits
Measurement error mitigation uses calibration matrices
ZNE extrapolates from amplified noise to zero noise
Qiskit Runtime has built-in mitigation via resilience_level

lessons.title: Custom Transpilation
lessons.content:
Custom Transpilation

💡 Beyond Default Transpilation

Custom transpilation allows fine-grained control over how circuits are compiled. You can create custom passes and pass managers for specific optimization goals.

Transpiler Pass Types

Analysis Passes

Gather information without modifying the circuit

Example: Count gates, analyze depth

Transformation Passes

Modify the circuit structure

Example: Optimize gates, route qubits

Creating Custom Passes

from qiskit.transpiler import PassManager, AnalysisPass, TransformationPass
from qiskit.transpiler.basepasses import BasePass
from qiskit.dagcircuit import DAGCircuit

class CountGates(AnalysisPass):
    """Count gates by type"""
    def run(self, dag: DAGCircuit):
        gate_counts = {}
        for node in dag.op_nodes():
            gate_name = node.op.name
            gate_counts[gate_name] = gate_counts.get(gate_name, 0) + 1
        
        self.property_set['gate_counts'] = gate_counts
        return dag

class RemoveIdentities(TransformationPass):
    """Remove identity operations"""
    def run(self, dag: DAGCircuit):
        for node in dag.op_nodes():
            if node.op.name == 'id':
                dag.remove_op_node(node)
        return dag

# Use custom passes
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit

qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.id(0)  # Identity gate
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.id(1)

pm = PassManager([CountGates(), RemoveIdentities(), CountGates()])
result = pm.run(qc)

print(f"After removing identities: {pm.property_set['gate_counts']}")
print(result.draw())

Custom Pass Manager

from qiskit.transpiler import PassManager
from qiskit.transpiler.passes import (
    Unroller, Optimize1qGates, CXCancellation,
    CommutativeCancellation, RemoveBarriers
)

def create_custom_pm(basis_gates=['cx', 'u1', 'u2', 'u3']):
    """Create a custom optimization pass manager"""
    pm = PassManager()
    
    # Stage 1: Unroll to basis gates
    pm.append(Unroller(basis_gates))
    
    # Stage 2: Optimize single-qubit gates
    pm.append(Optimize1qGates())
    
    # Stage 3: Cancel consecutive CX gates
    pm.append(CXCancellation())
    
    # Stage 4: Commutation-based cancellation
    pm.append(CommutativeCancellation())
    
    # Stage 5: Final single-qubit optimization
    pm.append(Optimize1qGates())
    
    return pm

# Test
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.cx(0, 1)  # Should be cancelled
qc.rz(0.5, 0)
qc.rz(0.3, 0)  # Should be combined

pm = create_custom_pm()
optimized = pm.run(qc)

print(f"Original depth: {qc.depth()}")
print(f"Optimized depth: {optimized.depth()}")
print(optimized.draw())

Staged Pass Manager

from qiskit.transpiler import StagedPassManager
from qiskit.transpiler.preset_passmanagers import generate_preset_pass_manager

# Get preset and modify
preset_pm = generate_preset_pass_manager(
    optimization_level=3,
    basis_gates=['cx', 'id', 'rz', 'sx', 'x']
)

# Create staged pass manager with custom stages
staged_pm = StagedPassManager(stages=['init', 'layout', 'routing', 'optimization'])

# Access individual stages
print(f"Stages: {staged_pm.stages}")

💡 When to Use Custom Transpilation

  • Targeting specific hardware constraints
  • Implementing novel optimization strategies
  • Debugging transpilation issues
  • Research on compilation techniques
keyTakeaways: Custom passes enable fine-grained transpilation control
Analysis passes gather information; Transformation passes modify circuits
PassManager chains multiple passes together
Use staged pass managers for complex compilation pipelines

lessons.title: Pulse-Level Control
lessons.content:
Pulse-Level Control

💡 Below the Gate Level

Gates are implemented via microwave pulses. Qiskit Pulse gives direct control over these pulses, enabling custom gates, optimal control, and quantum experiments beyond the gate model.

Gate vs Pulse Level

Gate Level

qc.x(0)  # X gate

Abstract operation

Pulse Level

with pulse.build():
  pulse.play(Drag(...))

Physical microwave pulse

Pulse Basics

from qiskit import pulse
from qiskit.pulse import library
import numpy as np

# Define a Gaussian pulse
gaussian = library.Gaussian(
    duration=160,      # samples
    amp=0.5,          # amplitude
    sigma=40,         # width
    name='my_gaussian'
)

# DRAG pulse (Derivative Removal by Adiabatic Gate)
drag = library.Drag(
    duration=160,
    amp=0.5,
    sigma=40,
    beta=0.5,         # DRAG correction
    name='my_drag'
)

# Visualize
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
gaussian.draw(ax=ax1)
ax1.set_title('Gaussian Pulse')
drag.draw(ax=ax2)
ax2.set_title('DRAG Pulse')
plt.show()

Building Pulse Schedules

from qiskit import pulse
from qiskit.pulse import library, DriveChannel, MeasureChannel

# Build a pulse schedule
with pulse.build(name='custom_x') as schedule:
    # Drive qubit 0
    drive_chan = DriveChannel(0)
    
    # Play X gate pulse
    pulse.play(
        library.Drag(duration=160, amp=0.5, sigma=40, beta=0.5),
        drive_chan
    )
    
    # Add delay
    pulse.delay(100, drive_chan)
    
    # Play another pulse
    pulse.play(
        library.Gaussian(duration=160, amp=0.3, sigma=40),
        drive_chan
    )

# Visualize schedule
schedule.draw()

Custom Gate Calibrations

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.circuit import Gate

# Define a custom gate
my_gate = Gate('my_x', 1, [])

# Create circuit with custom gate
qc = QuantumCircuit(1)
qc.append(my_gate, [0])

# Add calibration
with pulse.build() as custom_schedule:
    pulse.play(
        library.Drag(duration=160, amp=0.5, sigma=40, beta=0.5),
        DriveChannel(0)
    )

qc.add_calibration(my_gate, [0], custom_schedule)

# Now the circuit uses your custom pulse
print(qc.calibrations)

Applications

Optimal Control

Design pulses that minimize gate errors

Cross-Resonance Gates

Custom two-qubit gate implementations

Dynamical Decoupling

Apply pulse sequences to protect from decoherence

Characterization

Measure T1, T2, gate fidelities

⚠️ Note

Pulse-level control requires backend calibration data and is specific to each quantum device. Not all backends support pulse access.
keyTakeaways: Qiskit Pulse provides control below the gate abstraction
DRAG pulses reduce leakage errors
Custom calibrations can improve gate fidelity
Pulse access enables advanced experiments and optimization

lessons.title: Dynamic Circuits
lessons.content:
Dynamic Circuits

💡 Classical Control Flow

Dynamic circuits enable mid-circuit measurement and classical conditional operations. This unlocks algorithms requiring real-time feedback, like quantum error correction and teleportation.

Static vs Dynamic

Static Circuits

  • All gates predetermined
  • Measurement only at end
  • No classical feedback

Dynamic Circuits

  • Mid-circuit measurements
  • Classical conditionals (if/else)
  • Real-time feedback

Mid-Circuit Measurement

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, ClassicalRegister, QuantumRegister

# Create circuit with mid-circuit measurement
qr = QuantumRegister(2, 'q')
cr = ClassicalRegister(2, 'c')
qc = QuantumCircuit(qr, cr)

# Create entanglement
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)

# Mid-circuit measurement of qubit 0
qc.measure(0, 0)
qc.barrier()

# Continue computation on qubit 1
qc.h(1)
qc.measure(1, 1)

print(qc.draw())

Classical Conditionals

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit

qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)

# Prepare superposition
qc.h(0)
qc.measure(0, 0)

# Apply X on qubit 1 ONLY if measurement was 1
with qc.if_test((0, 1)):
    qc.x(1)

qc.measure(1, 1)

print(qc.draw())

Quantum Teleportation with Dynamic Circuits

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit

def teleportation_dynamic():
    qc = QuantumCircuit(3, 2)
    
    # Prepare state to teleport on q0
    qc.h(0)  # |+⟩ state
    qc.barrier()
    
    # Create Bell pair between q1 and q2
    qc.h(1)
    qc.cx(1, 2)
    qc.barrier()
    
    # Bell measurement on q0 and q1
    qc.cx(0, 1)
    qc.h(0)
    qc.measure([0, 1], [0, 1])
    qc.barrier()
    
    # Dynamic corrections on q2
    with qc.if_test((1, 1)):  # If c[1] == 1
        qc.x(2)
    with qc.if_test((0, 1)):  # If c[0] == 1
        qc.z(2)
    
    return qc

qc = teleportation_dynamic()
print(qc.draw())

Switch Statements

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit

qc = QuantumCircuit(3, 2)
qc.h([0, 1])
qc.measure([0, 1], [0, 1])

# Switch based on measurement outcome
with qc.switch(qc.clbits) as case:
    with case(0):  # 00
        qc.x(2)
    with case(1):  # 01
        qc.y(2)
    with case(2):  # 10
        qc.z(2)
    with case(3):  # 11
        qc.h(2)

print(qc.draw())

Applications

Quantum Error Correction

Measure syndromes and apply corrections in real-time

Quantum Teleportation

Classical corrections based on Bell measurement

Repeat-Until-Success

Retry operations until desired outcome

Qubit Reset

Measure and flip to return to |0⟩

💡 Hardware Support

Dynamic circuits require fast classical feedback. Check backend capabilities with backend.configuration().supported_features.
keyTakeaways: Dynamic circuits enable mid-circuit measurement
Classical conditionals (if_test, switch) control quantum operations
Essential for error correction and teleportation
Requires hardware support for fast classical feedback

lessons.title: Qiskit Lab: Real Backend
lessons.content:
🔬 Lab: Running on Real Quantum Hardware

🎯 Lab Objectives

  • Connect to IBM Quantum services
  • Select and characterize backends
  • Run circuits on real hardware
  • Apply error mitigation

Exercise 1: Connect to IBM Quantum

from qiskit_ibm_runtime import QiskitRuntimeService

# Save credentials (run once)
# QiskitRuntimeService.save_account(channel="ibm_quantum", token="YOUR_TOKEN")

# Load saved credentials
service = QiskitRuntimeService()

# List available backends
backends = service.backends()
for backend in backends:
    print(f"{backend.name}: {backend.num_qubits} qubits")

Exercise 2: Backend Selection

# Get least busy backend
from qiskit_ibm_runtime import QiskitRuntimeService

service = QiskitRuntimeService()

# Filter for suitable backends
backends = service.backends(
    filters=lambda b: b.status().operational
    and b.status().status_msg == 'active'
    and b.configuration().n_qubits >= 5
)

# Sort by queue length
least_busy = min(backends, key=lambda b: b.status().pending_jobs)
print(f"Selected: {least_busy.name} (Queue: {least_busy.status().pending_jobs} jobs)")

# Get backend properties
props = least_busy.properties()
print(f"\nQubit T1 times (μs):")
for i in range(min(5, least_busy.num_qubits)):
    t1 = props.t1(i) * 1e6 if props.t1(i) else 'N/A'
    print(f"  Q{i}: {t1:.1f}" if isinstance(t1, float) else f"  Q{i}: {t1}")

Exercise 3: Run on Real Hardware

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, transpile
from qiskit_ibm_runtime import SamplerV2 as Sampler

# Create Bell state circuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.measure_all()

# Transpile for backend
transpiled = transpile(qc, backend=least_busy, optimization_level=3)
print(f"Circuit depth after transpilation: {transpiled.depth()}")

# Run using Sampler primitive
sampler = Sampler(mode=least_busy)
job = sampler.run([transpiled], shots=1024)

print(f"Job ID: {job.job_id()}")
print("Waiting for results...")

result = job.result()
counts = result[0].data.meas.get_counts()
print(f"\nResults: {counts}")

Exercise 4: Error Mitigation

from qiskit_ibm_runtime import EstimatorV2 as Estimator, Options
from qiskit.quantum_info import SparsePauliOp

# Circuit without measurement
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)

observable = SparsePauliOp.from_list([("ZZ", 1.0)])

# With error mitigation
options = Options()
options.resilience_level = 2  # Enable ZNE
options.optimization_level = 3

estimator = Estimator(mode=least_busy, options=options)
job = estimator.run([(qc, observable)])
result = job.result()

mitigated_value = result[0].data.evs
print(f"⟨ZZ⟩ with mitigation: {mitigated_value}")
print(f"Ideal value: 1.0")

Exercise 5: Compare Simulator vs Hardware

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator

# Run on simulator
sim = AerSimulator()
sim_job = sim.run(qc, shots=1024)
sim_counts = sim_job.result().get_counts()

# Compare results
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))

ax1.bar(sim_counts.keys(), sim_counts.values())
ax1.set_title('Simulator (Ideal)')
ax1.set_ylabel('Counts')

ax2.bar(counts.keys(), counts.values())
ax2.set_title(f'Real Hardware ({least_busy.name})')
ax2.set_ylabel('Counts')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Calculate fidelity
ideal_prob_00 = sim_counts.get('00', 0) / 1024
real_prob_00 = counts.get('00', 0) / 1024
print(f"\nP(00) - Ideal: {ideal_prob_00:.3f}, Real: {real_prob_00:.3f}")

✅ Success Criteria

  • Successfully connect to IBM Quantum
  • Run circuit on real hardware
  • Observe noise effects vs simulator
  • Error mitigation improves results
keyTakeaways: QiskitRuntimeService connects to IBM Quantum backends
Transpilation optimizes circuits for specific hardware
Real hardware results show noise effects
Error mitigation (resilience_level) improves accuracy

lessons.title: Advanced Qiskit Quiz
lessons.content:
📝 Advanced Qiskit Assessment

📋 Quiz Instructions

Test your knowledge of advanced Qiskit features.

Question 1

What is the main advantage of Qiskit Runtime over traditional execution?

A) Better qubit quality
B) Reduced latency for iterative algorithms
C) More qubits available
D) Automatic error correction

Question 2

Which primitive computes expectation values of observables?

A) Sampler
B) Estimator
C) Transpiler
D) Composer

Question 3

What does Zero Noise Extrapolation (ZNE) do?

A) Removes all noise from the circuit
B) Amplifies noise and extrapolates to zero noise limit
C) Adds error correction codes
D) Uses more shots to average out noise

Question 4

What enables dynamic circuits?

A) Faster classical computers
B) Mid-circuit measurement and classical conditionals
C) More qubits
D) Better optimization levels

Question 5

What type of pulse is commonly used for single-qubit gates to reduce leakage?

A) Square pulse
B) DRAG pulse
C) Sine pulse
D) Triangle pulse

🎯 Answer Key

  1. B - Runtime reduces latency for iterative algorithms
  2. B - Estimator computes expectation values
  3. B - ZNE amplifies noise and extrapolates to zero
  4. B - Mid-circuit measurement and conditionals
  5. B - DRAG pulses reduce leakage errors
keyTakeaways: Runtime reduces iteration latency
Estimator computes expectation values
ZNE extrapolates from amplified noise
DRAG pulses minimize leakage
